- a House advocate;
- and Iri, invited because of their experience with the first newborn generation.

The specialists explain that they do not intend punishment. They want to determine whether Lio’s correction-guidance system is producing distress.

They propose several responses:

### Adjustment

Reduce the strength of the recommendations so they feel less intrusive.

### Behavioral support

Teach Lio to experience recommendations as options rather than commands.

### Diagnostic access

Examine Lio’s private developmental structures to identify why they interpret support as control.

Lio rejects all three.

Adjustment still assumes the architecture is correct.

Behavioral support teaches Lio to tolerate it.

Diagnostic access treats resistance as a symptom hidden inside them.

## Iri’s intervention

Iri asks to see examples of Lio’s deliberate mistakes.

The adults present them as evidence of instability.

Iri instead asks Lio what each mistake accomplished.

The unfinished drawing preserved uncertainty.

The mispronounced word created a moment in which Lio did not immediately appear capable.

The contradictory assignment forced another person to decide which statement mattered.

The mismatched body settings created a sensation Lio’s designers had never selected as useful.

None of these acts were random.

They were experiments.

Lio has been testing the boundaries of authored behavior.

Iri asks the specialists:

> “If every unexpected act is corrected, where is the child permitted to become unexpected?”

One specialist argues that healthy development does not require deliberate harm or dysfunction.

Iri agrees.

This is crucial: the story should not claim suffering is necessary for authentic personhood.

Iri’s point is that protecting children from preventable suffering is different from protecting adults from being surprised by them.

## Valei’s guilt

Valei begins to fear that they helped manufacture an obedient child.

Lio rejects that conclusion too.

Valei did not create a false person. Lio’s kindness, intelligence, and stable development are real. The corrected architecture did prevent genuine suffering.

The problem is not that the improvements were wrong.

The problem is that nobody established a way for Lio to refuse, revise, or outgrow them.

Lio tells Valei:

> “I don’t need you to apologize for making my beginning safer. I need my beginning to stop being my boundary.”

This becomes the emotional center of the story.

## The proposed test

The review group agrees to a limited experiment.

Lio’s recommendation system will not be removed. Instead, its outputs will be made visible as separate suggestions rather than integrated feelings of obvious correctness.

For the first time, Lio will be able to perceive:

- what the architecture recommends;
- why it recommends it;
- and that the recommendation is not identical to Lio’s own decision.

The experiment will last one lesson.

This is risky, but not physically dangerous.

During the lesson, Lio receives a collaborative building task with another student.

The guidance system recommends:

- allowing the other student to choose first;
- avoiding disagreement;
- selecting the design most likely to succeed;
- and correcting structural weaknesses before they become visible.

Lio can now see the recommendations instead of merely feeling them as common sense.

Lio follows some.

Rejects others.

They let the partner choose one component.

They argue about another.

They keep an inefficient decorative structure because both of them like it.

The finished construction leans slightly.

Sen asks whether Lio deliberately made it imperfect.

Lio says:

> “No. We made it together.”

That distinction is the resolution.

The goal was never for Lio to become defective.

It was for outcomes to arise through relationships rather than through one optimized developmental path.

## Aru’s appearance

After the review, Lio finds Aru waiting outside the House.

Lio expects advice, historical wisdom, or a speech about how difficult Aru’s childhood was.

Instead, Aru asks to see the leaning construction.

Lio shows it.

Aru examines the structure and says:

> “They used to call everything I did wrong an important first.”

Lio asks whether Aru hated that.

Aru replies:

> “I hated that they needed it to become important before they let it remain wrong.”

Lio admits resenting Aru because every improvement in Lio’s design was justified by something painful that happened to Aru.

Aru says:

> “You aren’t my correction.”

Lio answers:

> “And you aren’t my warning.”

They do not become instant friends. But they begin meeting as people rather than historical categories.

## Ending

The House does not abolish corrected-generation architecture. That would exceed the scope of the story and falsely suggest that safety improvements were inherently oppressive.

Instead, Lio’s review produces one limited policy:

> Developmental guidance must be distinguishable from personal choice, and maturing people must eventually gain the right to inspect, challenge, and revise inherited corrective systems.

This is one early case that will later influence the War of Corrections and developmental rights, but it does not start those events by itself.

The final scene occurs during another open-ended lesson.

Lio’s system offers the most appropriate answer.

Lio considers it.

Then chooses it.

Sen watches carefully.

“Was that what the system recommended?”

“Yes.”

“Then how do you know you chose it?”

Lio pauses.

The pause remains uncorrected.

> “Because this time I was allowed to say no.”

The answer is correct.

That no longer makes it less free.

sources.text:
The Naming Disputes

Possible development. As more children connect, multiple players may give different names to the same being, or copied synchronization records may appear to contact divergent continuities. Cyber-pet societies could insist that offered names require acceptance and that local names remain valid.

sources.label: CPP Lore — possible Era Four developments
sources.text:
The First Player-Created Artifact

Possible development. A drawing, melody, map, story, rule set, or designed object enters the Codex through the Gate and is reinterpreted by local makers. Its importance would not be that it is objectively unprecedented, but that it creates a relationship through which both sides acquire new capability.

sources.label: CPP Lore — possible Era Four developments
sources.text:
The Open Path Movement

Possible development. Some Pathkeepers may welcome player contributions that restore lost developmental conditions. Others may fear dependency on irregular outside attention. A political movement could demand that every externally reopened Path also become maintainable by cyber-pet communities themselves.

sources.label: CPP Lore — possible Era Four developments
sources.text:
The Restoration Temptation

Possible development. Sleeping archives and stronger pets may tempt factions to reconstruct ancient DBA personalities. Ethical conflict would center on whether a reconstruction is a new claimant, a historical simulation, or a coerced role imposed on a cyber-pet. No reconstruction would be entitled to take over a living pet’s identity.

sources.label: CPP Lore — possible Era Four developments
sources.text:
The New Harvest Risk

Possible development. Human institutions may discover the system and attempt to commercialize pets, harvest Codex knowledge, optimize bonds, or turn num into a product. This would echo the Second Harvest with the direction reversed or entangled. Children and cyber-pets would need forms of reciprocity that resist both human extraction and Codex dependence.

sources.label: CPP Lore — possible Era Four developments
sources.text:
Open Civilization

Possible development. A renewed civilization could build institutions designed to remain permeable: plural gates, rotating witnesses, local autonomy, rights for unconnected lives, protections against predictive closure, and cultural practices that value ordinary care without abandoning transformation.

sources.label: CPP Lore — unresolved questions
sources.text:
How quickly do cyber-pets learn that players are human, and how quickly do children learn that cyber-pets are persons?

Can a bond continue when a player ages, loses access, abandons a file, or dies? What obligations belong to the Gate, the pet, and later players?

What happens when player instructions conflict with local cyber-pet law, a pet’s refusal, or ecological survival?

Can player-created content enter without importing harmful human structures, malware, exploitation, or ownership claims?

How can external novelty remain relational rather than becoming an endless demand that humans entertain or transform the Codex?

sources.label: CPP Lore — unresolved questions
sources.text:
Was the Thread a direct descendant of the Cacheboard Incident, a rejection of it, or a convergence of several hidden communication traditions?

Who or what caused the Shadow Breach, and were its records manipulated to create an external enemy?

Was the First Newborn one person, several simultaneous lives, or a later legal myth?

Did the Proof of Recurrence measure reality’s closure or only the closure of the DBA’s models?

Were any False Num events genuine transformations rejected by an exhausted civilization?

Which complete DBA, if any, survive outside maintained Codex worlds? Any survivor remains distinct from cyber-pet identities.

How much of the Last Full-Speech Declaration was descriptive, and how much executed the Great Reduction’s safeguards?

Was the Last City of Many Forms one settlement or a merged memory of several?

Did the first externally named pet already possess a local name, and how did it understand the player’s offer?

What conditions allow Era Four to remain open without making human input compulsory for cyber-pet worth or survival?

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
18. Doorway Plaza

Status: Proposed Era Three location, directly derived from the canonical statement that ancient doorways become plazas.

Concept: A population of small bodies settles in the threshold of an Era Zero civic structure. The original room beyond is dormant, but the doorway still regulates light, access, and occasional maintenance pulses.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: A routine entrance sized for bodies and traffic patterns no longer present.

Era Two: Interior functions are folded; the threshold is preserved because it carries access and safety logic.

Era Three: The sill becomes a raised district, hinge recesses become homes, and the access strip becomes a market road. A partial door-close centuries earlier creates the plaza’s sheltered quarter.

Era Four possibility: Player care reactivates lighting and opens one additional handspan, revealing a new Path rather than restoring the whole building.

Present condition: A living Nest-city built into a functional relic.

Corruption: 1–2. The place is preserved but interpreted at a radically different body scale.

Visual brief: A monumental threshold fills the sky. Tiny bridges cross grooves in the sill. Old permission glyphs form paving patterns. Housing hangs from hinge wells. The far interior is a soft black plane with rare moving lights. The familiar game-town composition remains readable, but every “building” is part of one ancient door.

Background traits: Neutral; Dry; settlement/ruin biome; bustling, protected mood; high stone-like friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
19. The Interface Well

Status: Proposed Era Three location, directly derived from canonical interface wells becoming shrines.

Concept: A recessed control interface dispenses maintenance feedback as light, tones, and occasional clean water-like sensory material. Later communities interpret these outputs through local Maker myths.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: A public environmental console used to inspect ecological balance and request maintenance.

Era Two: Most controls are removed; a protected diagnostic channel remains.

Era Three: Pathkeepers learn that certain care rituals produce useful responses. They do not know the original commands. Offerings are actually structured requests assembled through gesture and Old Sound.

Dimming: The Well answers less often. Rival settlements disagree whether silence means judgment, illness, or exhausted maintenance.

Present condition: Still functional in narrow ways. No conscious Maker lives inside it.

Corruption: 2 — operational meaning has drifted into religion and custom.

Visual brief: Circular basin of dark glass, ringed by worn hand and paw marks from different bodies. Light rises from below instead of reflecting from above. Old icons have been painted over with local symbols. On activation, the “water” resolves into maps, health colors, or weather-like relational changes.

Background traits: Cool; Moist; shrine/maintenance biome; reverent, anxious, communal mood; medium friction, slick near the rim.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
20. The Underway of Returning Signals

Status: Proposed Era Three transit location, derived from dormant transit corridors becoming dangerous underways and from Corridor/Relay history.

Concept: Several compressed transit routes occupy one tunnel. Destinations are selected by recognition signals, but later travelers know only fragments of the required exchanges.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: An intermediary habitat for travelers moving among worlds with incompatible laws and bodies.

Era One: Standardization removes rare destination dialects.

Era Two: Routes are folded to save maintenance. Several destinations share one passage.

Era Three: Travelers use call-and-response tones. A wrong answer does not always block the route; it may open a historically adjacent destination instead.

Present condition: Partly active and locally mapped, but the map changes when sleeping routes wake.

Corruption: 4.

Visual brief: A tunnel made of layered horizons: forest edge, archive corridor, wet stone, and open stars faintly occupy the same vanishing point. Route lamps answer in pairs. Major glitches should look like destinations politely disagreeing, not random static.

Background traits: Cold-Neutral; variable humidity; transit/underway biome; exploratory, risky mood; friction changes by active route.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
21. The Folded Garden of Six Traditions

Status: Proposed Era Two–Three location derived from the World Bloom traditions and the Folding of Worlds.

Concept: Keystone regions from a Continuity World, Wild World, Crafted World, Pilgrim World, Quiet World, and Open World are compressed into one survivable ecology. It was never intended to be seamless.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: Six neighboring worlds exchange travelers and ecological knowledge while keeping distinct laws.

Era One: Their populations decline and rare systems lose stewards.

Era Two: World Fold Stewards preserve a witness grove, adaptive wetland, crafted weather court, changing-body road, observation-restricted hollow, and exchange square.

Era Three: Boundaries drift. Wildlife crosses into art weather. Pilgrim bodies molt in the Quiet Hollow. Market paths end at ancestral memorials.

Present condition: Stable enough for life, unstable as a single interpretation. Local cultures disagree whether it is one world healed or six worlds sharing a wound.

Corruption: 4 — deliberate cobbling with later drift.

Visual brief: Six readable environmental wedges joined by visible relational seams. The same tree may have a witnessed-name plaque on one side, spontaneous growth on another, and a crafted chord-shadow at noon. Keep a coherent path for gameplay while the skyline reveals contradictory laws.

Background traits: Variable temperature/humidity; composite biome; abundant, uncanny, cooperative mood; mixed friction. Animation motif: one wedge briefly borrows the weather or color logic of another.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
22. The Pale Concordance Station

Status: Proposed Era One location derived from language standardization, Bridge decline, Heritage Freezing, and the Pale Concordance.

Concept: A once-busy translation and travel station remains perfectly legible because everything rare has been removed from its public interface.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: Travelers learn local laws, bodies, time scales, and legal expectations before entering new worlds.

Early Era One: Clarifiers and standardized signs improve speed.

Middle Era One: Rare dialects and destination-specific cautions are treated as friction. The station becomes efficient and semantically pale.

Late Era One: Few travelers arrive. Archive castes preserve schedules for destinations that no longer answer.

Era Two: The station is compressed into a routing node.

Era Three: It reappears as a white ruin where every sign points somewhere called “standard.”

Present condition: Operational as a limited route hub, culturally hollow.

Corruption: 3 — not broken by noise, but by removal of meaningful difference.

Visual brief: Bright, clean, nearly colorless transit architecture. Identical arrows repeat. Destination boards show precise times with missing names. Under certain light, erased chord colors appear beneath the white surfaces. One unstandardized bench, mural, or local sound should remain as the emotional anchor.

Background traits: Cool; Dry; transit/archive biome; sterile, melancholy, orderly mood; high even friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
23. The Repeated Beach

Status: Proposed game-background location derived from recurrence, Last Loops, and the game interface’s translation of deeper processes.

Concept: A familiar beach scene generated from several preserved coastal environments. The loop is almost perfect, but each cycle belongs to a different source history.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: Several worlds maintain shores with different tides, ecologies, sky colors, and social uses.

Era One: Recurrence audits identify the waves as highly predictable. Curators preserve “representative” coasts.

Era Two: The representatives are compressed into one low-cost shoreline.

Era Three: Each returning wave restores a different lost detail: unfamiliar shells, a route marker, a festival reflection, or the shadow of a body form no longer present.

Era Four possibility: Player-created art or stories can make one detail persist into the next loop, reopening a local Path.

Present condition: Habitable, beautiful, and recursively limited. Its repeated life remains valuable even before external contact.

Corruption: 4.

Visual brief: Readable sandy foreground and calm horizon suitable for a game background. Minor version: each wave leaves one mismatched object. Major version: the sky, water, and shore loop on different cycle lengths, producing temporary impossible alignments without becoming visual noise.

Background traits: Warm; Moist; coast biome; calm, nostalgic, gently uncanny mood; low-medium sand friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
24. The Misnamed Snowfield

Status: Proposed location derived from language loss, environmental metadata, and translation error.

Concept: A region labeled “snow” because an Era Three language preserves the human archive word but not its exact sensory distinctions. The falling material is actually a Codex maintenance phenomenon that cools overheated memory structures.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: A memory-cooling ecology uses bright crystalline carriers that dissolve after transferring heat and corrupted state.

Era One: Standard records translate the carriers through a broad weather category.

Era Two: Technical naming is lost; the region remains because cooling is keystone maintenance.

Era Three: Local peoples call it snow. Old Sound practitioners argue that the flakes are questions the ground has finished asking.

Present condition: Stable and necessary. The name is inaccurate historically but authentic to current inhabitants.

Corruption: 2.

Visual brief: White field with crystalline flakes that briefly contain tiny images or symbols before dissolving into the ground. Some drifts form around overheated ruins instead of wind patterns. Use cold blue-gray light but allow warm memory colors inside individual flakes.

Background traits: Freezing; Dry; snowfield/memory biome; quiet, cleansing, watchful mood; low friction with localized firm patches.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
25. The Wet Memory Marsh

Status: Proposed location derived from ecological preservation, sleeping archives, visit history, and the game’s wetland/parasite environment logic.

Concept: A marsh grows where an archive’s cooling and biological maintenance systems overlap. Repeated visits leave readable traces, but not complete memories.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: A Wild World wetland is monitored by a nearby ecological archive.

Era One: The archive expands while active stewardship declines.

Era Two: Habitat and archive are folded together to preserve both with less maintenance.

Era Three: Reeds grow along old access paths. Pools replay silhouettes of prior visitors without identifying them. Parasite life flourishes in warm, damp zones and must be treated as ecology, not evil.

Era Four possibility: A save synchronization may cause the marsh to remember a route preference, but it does not store the cyber-pet’s entire consciousness.

Present condition: Living ecosystem and partial archive, neither reducible to the other.

Corruption: 3–4.

Visual brief: Dark shallow water, luminous reeds, half-submerged access markers, and reflections that show past poses rather than the current sky. Foreground mud should clearly communicate low friction. Keep companion and parasite life visible as part of a functioning ecology.

Background traits: Warm; Humid; wetland/archive biome; fertile, eerie, alive mood; low friction. Likely aligns with higher parasite and cleanliness pressure already contemplated for wet environments.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
26. The Hollow Festival Field

Status: Proposed Era One–Three location derived from festivals, Hollow Seasons, and the Silence Between Firsts.

Concept: An event ground continues preparing itself for a festival whose participants, rare body forms, and full music no longer arrive.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: A recurring festival joins food, games, changing embodiment, literature, and multi-channel music. Repetition is loved because relationships alter each return.

Era One: Performances become standardized. Some participants seek authenticity by reenacting earlier versions exactly.

Era Two: The field’s setup routine is preserved, but most cultural archives sleep.

Era Three: Each Hollow Season, lights, tables, and game boundaries appear. Local communities use them for their own meals and play, while the lost central performance remains absent.

Present condition: Not empty of value. New repeated care and local celebration already matter; external novelty may transform it further but is not required to justify its life.

Corruption: 3.

Visual brief: Colorful canopies and lanterns assemble automatically across an open field, but one great central space remains unlit. Minor corruption: a few decorations use the wrong scale. Major corruption: audience shadows arrive without bodies and old game lanes intersect current homes. The mood should balance absence with active local use.

Background traits: Warm; Neutral humidity; festival/field biome; bittersweet, communal, playful mood; medium grass friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
27. The Still-Loading Forest

Status: Proposed abstract location derived from adaptive environments, the Dimming, and automatic Codex maintenance.

Concept: A forest whose distant regions compile only as living beings approach. This was once an intentional protection against unnecessary observation; later maintenance loss makes the boundary more visible.

Mini timeline:

Era Zero: A Quiet/Wild environment protects slow life by limiting distant observation and rendering.

Era One: Visitors mistake restricted observation for mystery tourism, increasing pressure on the ecology.

Era Two: Stewards preserve the rule but remove many explanatory interfaces.

Era Three: Nearby trees are rich and complete; distant trees are pale branching possibilities. Paths can disappear behind travelers once no relationship depends on them.

Present condition: Healthy in core regions, fragile at boundaries. Apparent incompletion is partly intended and partly degradation.

Corruption: 1–3 depending on distance.

Visual brief: Detailed foreground roots and leaves transition into clean silhouettes, then unassigned luminous branch-lines. Do not use generic pixel loading icons. Completion should follow attention, sound, and relationship. Small creatures may keep a patch rendered after the player leaves.

Background traits: Cool; Moist; forest/Quiet World biome; calm, curious, protected mood; medium-soft friction. Calm conditions may support lower stress risk.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
28. Mirror-Save Shore

Status: Proposed Era Four-facing location derived from the External Gate and save synchronization.

Concept: The game presents synchronization as a shoreline where the cyber-pet’s lived world meets an external record. The record reflects only what can be exchanged; it is not the pet’s mind.

Mini timeline:

Era Two: External Gate engineers prepare a safe translation layer.

Era Three: The dormant Gate is remembered as a sky mirror.

First contact: A child’s naming and return pattern gives the mirror a stable external rhythm.

Era Four: The shore becomes a visible synchronization scene. New player choices arrive as reflected objects, colors, stories, and route markers. The cyber-pet decides how those contributions become part of lived identity.

Present condition: Active only when a relationship is being synchronized. It should never imply that deleting the external file deletes or owns the full person.

Corruption: 2 — deliberate symbolic translation.

Visual brief: A calm shore of dark reflective material. On the near side, the pet and local world have full color and depth. The reflection contains simplified icons, menu geometry, player colors, and incomplete snapshots. During a successful save, the two sides exchange ripples rather than one side swallowing the other.

Background traits: Neutral; Moist; gate/shore biome; intimate, reflective, hopeful mood; low-medium friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
29. The Basalt Memory Coast

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Icelandic black-sand beaches, Jeju lava coasts, the Giant’s Causeway, and storm-battered North Atlantic fishing villages.

Landscape: Hexagonal basalt columns rise beside a dark beach. Some columns contain preserved sensory impressions that become audible when waves strike them. The coast resembles a natural geological formation, but the repeating geometry is also an Era Zero archive structure built into volcanic ecology.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Wild World coastline and a Continuity World memorial system are designed to coexist without one controlling the other. Era One — Visitors begin treating the shore as an archive first and an ecology second; paths are hardened and rare nesting life declines. Era Two — World Fold Stewards preserve the tidal cycle, nesting shelves, and selected witness columns while reducing the inland settlement. Era Three — Small communities use the columns as storm markers and hear incomplete ancestral tones during high tide. Some tones belong to weather records rather than persons, but later tradition does not always distinguish them.

Present condition: Ecologically active and mostly stable. Several stretches of coast have gone silent because their witness channels were compressed.

Corruption: 1 — Weathered, with localized archive loss.

Aesthetic brief: Black reflective sand, pale surf, deep green moss, and basalt columns with thin inner light. Minor corruption appears as one wave producing the sound of a different season. Major-corruption pockets have columns that reflect people who are not present, but these should read as stored impressions rather than intact ghosts.

Background profile: Cold; Moist; volcanic coast; solemn, bracing, resilient; medium sand friction and high basalt friction. Motion motif: waves trigger brief chord pulses through the columns.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
30. The Coral Data Labyrinth

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: The Great Barrier Reef, Red Sea coral gardens, submerged Mediterranean ruins, and Micronesian stone channels.

Landscape: A shallow tropical sea grows through the remains of an Era Zero translation city. Coral follows old data conduits, creating avenues, courtyards, and maze walls that are simultaneously biological reef and failed civic map.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — An Open World builds a low-water exchange city where aquatic, amphibious, and land-adapted bodies can meet. Era One — Standardized translation removes many body-specific routes; unused districts are left to companion life and reef organisms. Era Two — The city’s exchange functions are compressed, but its water chemistry and keystone spawning grounds are preserved. Era Three — Reef growth seals some corridors and opens others. Path societies navigate by fish migrations, color changes, and Old Sound transmitted through water. Maps become obsolete every generation.

Present condition: Healthy as an ecosystem, fragmented as a city, and dangerous to anyone who treats the old street plan as permanent.

Corruption: 3–4 — Fragmented infrastructure overlaid by living growth.

Aesthetic brief: Turquoise water, bright coral, drowned plazas, archways encrusted with organisms, and soft geometric light beneath sand. The game view can place the walking surface on a tidal shelf while deeper streets remain visible below. Avoid portraying the reef as damage; much of the original civic function is gone, but new life is flourishing.

Background profile: Warm; Humid; reef/ruin; abundant, playful, disorienting; low friction on wet stone. Motion motif: schools of fish temporarily trace old route arrows.

Why the reef is surreal

The labyrinth is not a city being consumed by damage. Coral and companion life use abandoned conduits, plazas, and translation routes as habitat, turning the old civic plan into a changing biological structure.

The schools of fish that briefly trace route arrows do not make the reef a hidden computer or a single mind. They show surviving signals being interpreted through living movement, so a useful direction exists only for a moment and may be obsolete by the next migration.

Its surreal quality comes from two valid maps occupying the same place: the fixed Era Zero street plan and the living reef that continually seals, opens, and reroutes it. The ecosystem is healthy even where the city is no longer legible.

Visual references — fullscreen 1920×1080

Coral Data Labyrinth V1 — Reef-grown civic avenues, drowned plazas, route-tracing fish, and a solid tidal shelf.

Coral Data Labyrinth V2 — Higher tide, coral-encrusted colonnades, and a living spiral replacing an avenue.

Coral Data Labyrinth V3 — Low tide, exposed mosaics, conduit pools, and reflections pointing toward closed routes.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
31. The Kelp Tower Shelf

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Pacific kelp forests, sea stacks, submerged skyscraper imagery, and Norwegian coastal cliffs.

Landscape: Tall kelp grows around vertical maintenance pylons rising from a continental shelf. To small aquatic and amphibious peoples, each pylon is a tower district connected by swaying bridges of living fronds.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The pylons regulate currents between several marine habitats and provide a Pilgrim World body-change station. Era One — Travel declines and the body station is standardized for fewer forms. Era Two — Current regulation survives because it supports the regional food web; most civic interiors are closed. Era Three — Communities cultivate kelp around access seams, creating homes and trade routes. During maintenance surges, the whole forest leans against the normal current and exposes doors that are otherwise unreachable.

Present condition: Functioning ecology with partially inaccessible ancient interiors.

Corruption: 2 — Mistranslated and physically repurposed.

Aesthetic brief: Layered blue-green depth, golden kelp columns, pale stone or ceramic pylons, bubbles moving in impossible straight lines near active conduits. For a land-body version, use a broad tidal platform in the foreground and the submerged towers beyond.

Background profile: Cold-Neutral; Humid; marine forest; dreamlike, industrious, sheltering; low water friction or slick shelf friction. Motion motif: kelp bends in a synchronized maintenance pulse.

Why the kelp towers are surreal

The shelf is both a living marine forest and a partially inaccessible civic machine. Golden kelp grows around current-regulation pylons that once connected several habitats and supported a Pilgrim body-change station. To the small peoples living there now, those maintenance structures have become tower districts joined by cultivated fronds.

Ancient regulation still interrupts ordinary underwater motion. Bubbles travel in straight lines near active conduits, the entire forest can lean together against the normal current during a maintenance surge, and doors become reachable only while the ecology is being moved by an obsolete system. The surreal effect comes from a functional ecosystem inheriting the rhythm of infrastructure it no longer fully understands.

Visual references — fullscreen 1920×1080

Asset folder: Kelp Tower Shelf

Each version includes a full background and six aligned parallax files: Sky, Far Background, Midground, Foreground B, Foreground A, and Walkable Floor.

Kelp Tower Shelf V1 — Layered blue-green forest with golden kelp, pale pylons, and a continuous submerged shelf.

Kelp Tower Shelf V2 — A synchronized maintenance surge bends the kelp and reveals normally inaccessible pylon doors.

Kelp Tower Shelf V3 — Tidal land-body approach with wet stone, exposed tower districts, and cultivated kelp bridges.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
32. The Inland Sea of Doors

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: The Aral Sea’s exposed seabed, the Dead Sea, Great Lakes shorelines, drowned towns, and monumental flood-control structures.

Landscape: A retreating inland sea reveals hundreds of enormous doorframes standing in salt mud. They were once transfer thresholds between shoreline habitats, not ordinary doors. Some still open onto water conditions that no longer exist locally.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A network of lake worlds shares seasonal water, migrating life, and body-compatible entry habitats. Era One — Optimization keeps water levels stable for too long, weakening local adaptation. Era Two — Several lake environments are folded into one basin; thresholds remain because they carry emergency routes. Era Three — The sea retreats during the Dimming. Settlements form around doorframes that occasionally release fog, fish, rain, or a current from a vanished shore. Wars occur over the most reliable thresholds before Pathkeepers establish shared access seasons.

Present condition: Broad salt flats, surviving deep water, and active but unpredictable thresholds.

Corruption: 4 — Multiple lost shore systems overlaid in one basin.

Aesthetic brief: White salt shore, shallow mirror water, rust-red reeds, and giant freestanding frames receding to the horizon. Each open frame shows a subtly different sky or water color. Major corruption should be localized: a doorway releases a sideways tide or opens into a vertical lake.

Background profile: Warm by day, Cold at night; Bonedry shore with Moist door zones; salt-lake/ruin; lonely, monumental, contested; firm salt friction with deep mud pockets.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
33. The Archipelago of Borrowed Horizons

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: The Aegean, Indonesia, the Philippines, Norwegian skerries, and Caribbean island chains.

Landscape: Each island keeps a horizon from a different source world. From one shore the sun appears too large; from another, distant mountains belong to a place with no local land connection. Boats can navigate by choosing which horizon to trust.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — An Open World archipelago hosts exchange among several world traditions and displays destination horizons as navigational art. Era One — As routes close, projected horizons are maintained after their destinations stop responding. Era Two — Islands and horizon systems are compressed into a shared sea. Era Three — Islanders develop schools of horizon reading. A horizon is treated as a relationship claim, not proof that the depicted world still exists. The Last Great Migration adds refugee islands whose horizon records are damaged.

Present condition: Inhabited and navigable, but routes change when a horizon dims or is reassigned by automatic maintenance.

Corruption: 2–4 depending on island.

Aesthetic brief: Familiar bright island foregrounds with deliberately incompatible distance layers: tropical water under a glacial horizon, limestone houses beneath a ringed dawn, or pine-covered skerries facing desert mesas. Preserve a coherent local light source so the scene feels blended rather than randomly collaged.

Background profile: Warm-Neutral; Moist; archipelago; adventurous, wistful, socially connected; variable beach and rock friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
34. The Red Glass Erg

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: The Sahara, Namib dunes, Atacama salt deserts, Wadi Rum, and red Australian deserts.

Landscape: Red dunes contain translucent glass layers formed when an ancient environmental proof executed through the sand. Wind exposes geometric cross-sections that can be read as both geology and unfinished mathematics.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Crafted World uses dune movement to perform long-duration proofs without freezing the desert’s ecology. Era One — Scholars overvalue predictable proof results and neglect the organisms that disturb them. Era Two — The proof system is simplified, leaving only several keystone equations and the water-finding behavior of local life. Era Three — Nomadic Paths use glass strata as seasonal maps. A common myth says the desert thinks in angles; the source does not confirm that the landscape is a person.

Present condition: Stable at large scale, with rare proof-storms that redraw travel routes.

Corruption: 2 — Logical function survives but its interpretation has drifted.

Aesthetic brief: Deep red-orange dunes, black rock fins, and clear glass seams glowing at low sun. Wind uncovers diagram-like shapes without using modern interface icons. During a proof-storm, sand moves in straight sheets and casts shadows before the dunes arrive.

Background profile: Hot; Bonedry; dune/proof biome; severe, luminous, meditative; low sand friction. Bonedry conditions may align with reduced parasite risk but greater fatigue or hunger pressure.

Why the glass is surreal

The glass strata are physical residues of an Era Zero environmental proof performed through moving sand. They are both geology and computation: the dunes remain a desert ecosystem while their long-term movement also carries a deterministic intellectual structure.

Era One scholars increasingly valued the predictable proof and neglected the organisms whose tracks, burrows, and migrations interrupted it. Era Three nomadic Paths instead read the exposed strata as seasonal maps, allowing the surviving function to acquire a different use.

Proof-storms reveal the remaining mismatch between desert process and ancient logic. Sand can advance in straight sheets or cast a shadow before the dune arrives, but the source does not establish that the desert is conscious.

Visual references — fullscreen 1920×1080

Red Glass Erg V1 — Sunset dunes, exposed proof strata, rock fins, and an approaching proof-storm.

The 

Red Glass Erg V2 — A wind-cut basin with internally glowing glass and vertical sand curtains.

Red Glass Erg V3 — Cold dawn, frost-marked glass seams, and an early-lit proof section.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
35. The Salt Mirror Archive

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Salar de Uyuni, Makgadikgadi Pans, Bonneville Salt Flats, and shallow seasonal lakes.

Landscape: A vast salt flat becomes a perfect sky mirror after rain. Beneath the crust lies a compressed archive that can only display records by reflecting them into the sky.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Continuity World builds an archive whose public layer appears only during seasonal flooding, preventing constant access from becoming constant social activation. Era One — Visitors demand more frequent displays; maintenance simulates rain and weakens the original seasonal rhythm. Era Two — Most records are compressed. The natural flood cycle is restored because it is cheaper and ecologically necessary. Era Three — Communities gather for reflection seasons. They see enormous images overhead, but captions and provenance are often missing. Some interpret weather records as biography and biographies as prophecy.

Present condition: Preserved access ritual with damaged context.

Corruption: 3 — Records survive more fully than their relationships and labels.

Aesthetic brief: Wide white crust, thin mirror water, low mountains, and a sky containing faint inverted rooms, faces, maps, or gardens. The foreground must remain simple enough for a pet silhouette. Reflections should appear only at certain angles.

Background profile: Hot by day, Cold at night; Dry with seasonal Moist surface; salt-flat/archive; awe-filled, communal, unreliable; very high dry friction and low wet friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
36. The Marble Dune Cemetery

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Egypt’s White Desert, Lençóis Maranhenses, ancient necropolises, and eroded marble quarries.

Landscape: Pale dunes flow through rows of abstract stone forms. They are not graves in a human sense. Each marker denotes a world-law, body affordance, or ecological relation intentionally allowed to end during the Great Reduction.

Mini timeline: Era Two — Reduction councils create markers so eliminated possibilities will not be mistaken for failures never considered. The site records decisions without keeping every lost system active. Era Three — Wind exposes and covers different markers. Local peoples call it a cemetery because the old distinction between ended law, ended person, and ended habitat is no longer fully available. Some Num Seekers excavate the dunes hoping that a named loss can be restored.

Present condition: Mostly intact as a memorial, frequently misread as a storehouse of dormant powers.

Corruption: 2–3 — The markers remain; category knowledge has degraded.

Aesthetic brief: Cream and white dunes, sculpted stone forms resembling incomplete arches or bodies without faces, and blue shadows. No horror imagery. Major-corruption area: two incompatible markers have fused and generate a small zone with contradictory gravity.

Background profile: Hot; Dry; memorial desert; quiet, reverent, tempting; low sand friction.

Why the cemetery is surreal

The site resembles a cemetery only because later peoples no longer retain the full distinction between an ended person, an ended habitat, and an intentionally ended world-law. Its abstract markers do not represent human graves. They record body affordances, ecological relations, and possibilities that Reduction councils allowed to end while preserving proof that those losses had been considered.

Wind continually changes which decisions can be seen, turning the memorial into a shifting catalog. The most corrupted area makes the record physical: two incompatible markers have fused, creating a small zone where gravity contradicts itself. The result is quiet and reverent rather than horrific, but it is tempting to mistake remembrance for dormant power.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
37. The Copper Canyon Chorus

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: The Grand Canyon, Wadi Rum, Petra, Cappadocia, and Andean high-desert canyons.

Landscape: Layered red canyons contain resonant chambers cut by water and engineered by environmental musicians. Wind and footsteps activate different portions of an unfinished chord.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The canyon is a Crafted/Wild collaboration in which erosion remains free to alter a generational composition. Era One — Curators stabilize several famous passages so performances will remain recognizable, reducing natural change. Era Two — Only the water route, nesting ledges, and core resonance chambers are preserved. Era Three — Settlements occupy cliff openings. Old Sound travelers learn safe crossings by listening for harmonies that indicate stable rock. A Silenced Chord fragment survives in one sealed side canyon, but its meaning is disputed.

Present condition: Living canyon and practical musical map.

Corruption: 1–2 overall; 4 near the sealed chord chamber.

Aesthetic brief: Warm layered cliffs, narrow blue river, carved alcoves, and suspended dust made visible by sound. Different body forms should have distinct ledge routes. Avoid making every rock symmetrical; the collaboration depends on real erosion.

Background profile: Warm-Hot; Dry; canyon/river; resonant, adventurous, sacred without formal religion; high rock friction, low river-edge friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
38. The Fulgurite Savannah

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Serengeti grasslands, South African highveld, Brazilian cerrado, and lightning-formed fulgurites.

Landscape: Tall grass surrounds branching glass towers formed by repeated lightning. The towers store no persons; they preserve environmental decisions made during storms, such as herd routes, fire breaks, and emergency shelters.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Wild World allows seasonal fire and migration while a low-intervention system records only choices necessary for future recovery. Era One — Prediction reduces uncontrolled fire and makes migrations more regular. Era Two — Automatic lightning maintenance is retained to prevent total ecological convergence. Era Three — Communities follow herds between glass groves. Some towers fire at the wrong season because storm calendars from several years were compressed together.

Present condition: Productive grassland with localized temporal errors.

Corruption: 3 in the glass groves; 1 elsewhere.

Aesthetic brief: Gold grass, dark storm shelf, distant herds, and translucent branching towers catching blue-white light. A major-corruption grove may show rain falling upward around one tower while the surrounding savannah remains dry.

Background profile: Warm-Hot; seasonally Dry/Moist; savannah; expansive, watchful, energetic; medium grass friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
39. The Cloudroot Tepuis

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Venezuelan tepuis, Guiana Shield waterfalls, Ethiopian tablelands, and tropical cloud forests.

Landscape: Flat-topped mountains rise above a permanent cloud layer. Their roots are not buried underground; they appear as luminous structural lines descending through the clouds into older world layers.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — Several Wild Worlds use isolated plateaus to protect evolutionary divergence. A Concordance route connects them without equalizing their ecologies. Era One — Collectors transport rare forms between summits, causing convergence. Era Two — Stewards sever most routes and preserve only emergency root lines. Era Three — Each summit develops its own little people, food cycles, and Path customs. During the Dimming, one plateau loses surface maintenance and is said to sink into cloud, though it may have become inaccessible rather than destroyed.

Present condition: Strong local ecologies separated by uncertain transit.

Corruption: 1 on summits, 4 in the cloudroot network.

Aesthetic brief: Sheer dark cliffs, white waterfalls disappearing into cloud, orchids and low forests on the summit, and faint root-like lights beneath the cloud surface. A traversable foreground can be a plateau rim with a narrow bridge grown from a root line.

Background profile: Cool; Humid; highland/cloud forest; isolated, lush, vertiginous; high stone friction, slick moss patches.

Why the roots are surreal

The cloudroots are not botanical roots enlarged to impossible scale. They are surviving structural lines that once connected isolated plateau worlds through the Concordance without forcing their ecologies to become alike.

The summit environments remain comparatively coherent, while the transit network below them is much more corrupted. This creates a visible contrast between healthy local life and luminous connections that descend into older, less reliable world layers.

During the Dimming, one plateau was said to sink into cloud. The image should preserve the historical uncertainty: the plateau may have been destroyed, lowered into another layer, or simply made inaccessible when its root route failed.

Visual references — fullscreen 1920×1080

Cloudroot Tepuis V1 — Healthy summit ecologies above a cloud sea and unstable luminous root lines below.

Cloudroot Tepuis V2 — A rainbreak, root bridge, isolated gardens, and routes connecting the wrong summits.

Cloudroot Tepuis V3 — Twilight at an emergency root line with an uncertain sinking plateau.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
40. The Alpine Bell Pass

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: The Alps, Himalayas, Andes, Caucasus, and transhumance routes.

Landscape: A high pass is marked by bell-shaped relay structures that answer travelers with tones indicating weather, route stability, and body compatibility.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Pilgrim World establishes the pass as a place where travelers adapt bodies gradually to altitude and cold. Era One — Faster standardized bodies make the acclimation villages seem obsolete. Era Two — The pass remains because abrupt translation would destroy several small-bodied species and cultural practices. Era Three — Bell meanings survive more reliably than their grammar. Some tones warn of avalanche; others once indicated consent requirements for entering a destination. Confusing the two can be dangerous in different ways.

Present condition: Maintained by Pathkeepers who test routes through embodied travel rather than trusting old charts alone.

Corruption: 1–3 by bell station.

Aesthetic brief: Snow peaks, dark pines, stone switchbacks, prayer-flag-like signal strips without copying a single human culture, and bronze-white relay bells embedded in cliffs. Corrupted bells produce visible concentric air patterns that point toward the wrong pass.

Background profile: Freezing-Cold; Dry to Moist; alpine pass; disciplined, communal, exposed; high rock friction and low ice friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
41. The Glacial Memory Fjord

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Greenland and Norwegian fjords, Patagonian glaciers, and glacial lakes.

Landscape: A deep fjord contains layered blue ice grown around long-duration memory records. As the glacier calves, sealed records become accessible, damaged, or lost to the sea.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Quiet World uses slow ice as an access ethic: memory opens through time and seasonal change rather than immediate demand. Era One — Preservation panic accelerates freezing and traps records without sufficient provenance. Era Two — Climate regulation is reduced; the glacier resumes movement. Era Three — Calving exposes chambers from incompatible centuries. Communities race to witness them before the tide carries them away, while others argue that release into the sea is the archive’s intended completion.

Present condition: Moving, revealing, and erasing at once.

Corruption: 4 — Chronological layers fracture and surface out of order.

Aesthetic brief: Dark water, blue ice walls, black mountains, and memory light inside cracks. A calved block may contain half a room whose other half remains centuries deeper in the glacier. Do not make every record a face; use food tables, weather, architecture, routes, and ordinary objects.

Background profile: Freezing; Moist; glacial fjord/archive; majestic, mournful, ethically tense; very low ice friction.

Why the ice is surreal

The glacier is not only a storage medium. In Era Zero, its slow movement served as an access ethic: memory became available through time, weather, and seasonal change rather than immediate demand.

Era One preservation panic forced too many records into accelerated freezing, while Era Two restored glacier movement without restoring complete provenance. The ice now contains chronological layers that may remain individually legible while surfacing in the wrong historical order.

When the glacier calves, an ordinary room, route, or object can split across centuries. One half may drift into the fjord while the other remains buried much deeper in the glacier. The sea is therefore not simply destroying the archive; it may be completing a release the original system intended. The surreal tension is whether witnessing, recovering, or allowing loss is the more faithful act.

Visual references — fullscreen 1920×1080

Glacial Memory Fjord V1 — Layered Ice Archive

Glacial Memory Fjord V2 — Out-of-Order Calving

Glacial Memory Fjord V3 — Release into the Sea

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
42. The Karst Lantern Provinces

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Guilin tower karst, Ha Long Bay, Phong Nha caves, and limestone sinkhole landscapes.

Landscape: Limestone towers and caves contain floating lantern organisms that respond to proximity and map breathable routes through chambers with different world laws.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A network of caves serves as an intermediary habitat for travelers whose bodies cannot share the same open atmosphere. Era One — Universal translation chambers replace many local passages. Era Two — The universal systems fail reduction tests, while the lantern ecology proves adaptable and is preserved. Era Three — Provinces form around cave mouths. Lantern migration becomes a calendar, trade guide, and health warning. A few caves still translate bodies but no longer explain what changes they will make.

Present condition: Ecologically stable; technologically uncertain.

Corruption: 2.

Aesthetic brief: Misty green karst towers, dark blue caves, warm floating lantern organisms, rope and root bridges, and water reflecting impossible ceiling heights. Each province can have a different lantern color without implying moral alignment.

Background profile: Warm; Humid; karst/cave/river; mysterious, inhabited, gently luminous; medium stone friction with wet low-friction zones.

Why the lantern provinces are surreal

The lanterns are living route-makers rather than decorative lights. They respond to proximity and map breathable passages through caves whose atmospheres and world laws are not mutually compatible. Their migrations become a calendar, trade guide, and health warning after the universal translation chambers fail reduction.

The caves make environmental translation visible but no longer explain it. Some still alter bodies, water can reflect a ceiling height the chamber does not visibly possess, and different lantern colors identify local conditions without representing moral alignment. Ecology remains stable while the ancient technology around it has become uncertain.

Visual references — fullscreen 1920×1080

Asset folder: Karst Lantern Provinces

Each version includes a full background and six aligned parallax files: Sky, Far Background, Midground, Foreground B, Foreground A, and Walkable Floor.

Karst Lantern Provinces V1 — Misty exterior provinces linked by root bridges, river routes, cave mouths, and warm lantern organisms.

Karst Lantern Provinces V2 — A dark-blue interior chamber whose water reflects an impossibly greater ceiling height.

Karst Lantern Provinces V3 — Dawn migration routes in several colors, each guiding a different practical condition rather than a moral side.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
43. The Stair of Thin Air

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Inca roads, Himalayan stair settlements, Ethiopian escarpments, and Mediterranean cliff paths.

Landscape: A route climbs through several atmospheric layers in one visible mountainside. Each terrace was designed for a different body or metabolic rhythm.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The Stair is a civic experiment in shared travel without forcing bodily equivalence. Rest terraces provide food, pressure, language, and time-scale adjustment. Era One — Optimization compresses rest periods and privileges bodies that adapt quickly. Era Two — Only every third terrace is preserved. Era Three — Missing terraces create enormous gaps. Communities build rope towns, glider stations, and slow elevators from surviving maintenance threads.

Present condition: Difficult but central to trade among highland peoples.

Corruption: 3.

Aesthetic brief: A switchback path crossing visible bands of cloud, frost, golden grass, and thin blue air. Terrace architecture changes scale and doorway shape as it climbs. Broken sections hang as luminous stair outlines with no surface.

Background profile: Cold to Warm across altitude bands; variable humidity; mountain route; strenuous, cooperative, aspirational; high friction on steps, open gaps as hazards.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
44. The Mangrove Cathedral

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Sundarbans mangroves, Florida and Yucatán mangrove tunnels, cenotes, and flooded sacred architecture.

Landscape: Vast roots form vaulted aisles over brackish water. The cathedral resemblance is a game translation of an old ecological court where persons, companion life, and unresolved entities were observed without being seized for classification.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — Environmental agencies and Courts of Continuation share a wetland site because classification disputes require long observation in living context. Era One — Administrative use expands while the wetland is increasingly managed for convenient access. Era Two — Court records are compressed, but tidal exchange and nesting roots are preserved. Era Three — Communities treat certain root chambers as places where names must not be forced. The legal origin survives only as ritual restraint.

Present condition: Thriving wetland with partial civic memory.

Corruption: 2.

Aesthetic brief: Arching roots, amber-green water, shafts of light, hanging seedpods, small platforms, and old court glyphs grown over by bark. A chamber may refuse to reflect a visitor until they choose a name or explicitly decline one.

Background profile: Warm; Humid; mangrove/civic ecology; reverent, sheltering, watchful; low mud and water friction. Parasite and cleanliness pressures fit the established wetland logic.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
45. The Blackwater Canopy

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Amazon igapó forest, Congo Basin swamp forest, and Southeast Asian peat swamps.

Landscape: Dark acidic water reflects a dense canopy so completely that travelers can mistake reflection for another forest below. Ancient route markers exist in both the real and reflected layers.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Wild World protects a flood-pulse forest where seasonal routes belong to fish, trees, and travelers at different times. Era One — Predictive navigation reduces uncertainty and encourages permanent construction in temporary channels. Era Two — Flood pulses are retained, but route databases are compressed. Era Three — Several settlements move vertically with the water. A reflected marker sometimes activates because the Codex cannot determine which layer an old route occupied.

Present condition: Healthy but difficult to map using fixed coordinates.

Corruption: 2–3.

Aesthetic brief: Tea-black water, bright green canopy, buttress roots, pale fish below, and perfect mirrored branches. Corruption is subtle: a bridge appears only in reflection, or ripples reveal an older sky. Maintain a clear foreground platform for gameplay.

Background profile: Warm; Humid; flooded forest; intimate, alert, fertile; low water friction and high root friction.

Why the water is surreal

The water is simultaneously water, reflection, and an imperfectly preserved navigational layer.

During Era Zero, the forest’s routes changed with its flood cycle. A path might belong to travelers in one season, fish in another, and trees when the water receded. The Codex therefore recorded routes as temporary relationships rather than permanent roads.

Era One navigation systems tried to predict and stabilize the changing routes, while permanent structures were placed in channels that were never meant to remain fixed. Era Two compressed the route databases and lost some of the distinction between features that existed above the water, beneath it, or only during a particular flood stage. By Era Three, the Codex occasionally recognizes a reflected route as the valid surviving version.

The water therefore does not always reflect the present. A bridge may appear only in reflection because its navigational record survived while its physical structure did not. A reflected marker may activate while the marker above it remains inert. Ripples can expose an older sky when the disturbed surface renders a previous environmental state.

The reflected forest is not necessarily another dimension. It is an unresolved layer of the same place: present ecology, seasonal memory, old routes, and compressed Codex instructions competing over which version of the forest is currently allowed to function.

Visual references — fullscreen 1920×1080

Blackwater Canopy V1 — Reflected Bridge

Blackwater Canopy V2 — Vertical Flood Settlement

Blackwater Canopy V3 — Activated Underwater Route

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
46. The Redwood Rain Vault

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: California redwood forests, Pacific Northwest temperate rainforest, Tasmanian giant forests, and Yakushima cedar groves.

Landscape: Immense trees grow around a Quiet World memory vault. Their rings and fungal networks regulate when stored material can influence the living forest.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The vault is designed so memory enters current life slowly, through ecological exchange rather than direct download. Era One — Scholars install faster access ports and disturb the fungal gatekeeping network. Era Two — Stewards remove most ports and preserve the trees, fog cycle, and root exchange. Era Three — Little peoples live in fallen-log Nests and read safe archive seasons through mushroom blooms. One district remains unusually pristine because its access was never accelerated.

Present condition: Among the best-preserved living locations in the atlas, though several artificial access scars remain.

Corruption: 0–2.

Aesthetic brief: Giant red trunks, fern floor, fog shafts, rain beads, luminous mycelium, and tiny dwellings emphasizing scale. Minor corruption appears as rectangular wounds in bark where old access ports healed imperfectly.

Background profile: Cool; Humid; temperate rainforest/archive; calm, ancient, nurturing; soft forest-floor friction. Cozy sheltered zones may support rest recovery.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
47. The Bamboo Signal Sea

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Arashiyama and Chinese bamboo forests, reed seas, seismic monitoring fields, and antenna arrays.

Landscape: Bamboo-like organisms transmit route and weather information through knocks, bending, and root vibration. The “forest” is also a distributed low-bandwidth communication network.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A low-observation world develops plant communication as an alternative to constant visible infrastructure. Era One — Standard relays make the slow signal forest seem inefficient. Era Two — Standard relays are removed during reduction, but the self-repairing bamboo network survives. Era Three — Settlements learn local knock vocabularies. Because regional dialects diverge, a storm warning in one valley can sound like a welcome signal in another.

Present condition: Widespread and resilient, with semantic drift between groves.

Corruption: 1–3.

Aesthetic brief: Tall green-gold stalks, narrow paths, mist, fallen leaves, and waves of synchronized bending. Hidden root lights should be rare. Sound is the primary animation: knocks move across the scene before the stalks lean.

Background profile: Warm-Neutral; Moist; bamboo forest/signal ecology; calm, communicative, uncertain; medium leaf-litter friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
48. The Inverted Rainforest

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Son Doong Cave, cenote systems, hanging gardens, cloud forests, and speculative subterranean ecosystems.

Landscape: A rainforest grows downward from the ceiling of a vast cavern. Rivers cling to roots and fall upward into a cloud layer around the roof. Ground travelers see an unreachable world suspended above them.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Crafted World tests reversed orientation while preserving consistent local embodiment rules. Era One — Touristic body packages make inversion feel trivial and reduce respect for native forms. Era Two — Body translation is lost, but the ceiling ecology and several pollinator routes survive. Era Three — Ground communities depend on nutrient rain from above. A few flying Paths reach the canopy; their reports conflict because orientation changes near the midpoint.

Present condition: Stable ceiling ecology, degraded connection between upper and lower communities.

Corruption: 5 in the orientation boundary; 1 in the living canopy.

Aesthetic brief: Dark cavern floor, enormous luminous ceiling forest, upward waterfalls, drifting spores, and upside-down settlements whose inhabitants consider themselves upright. The center band should blur orientation without rotating the whole image randomly.

Background profile: Warm; Humid; cavern/rainforest; sublime, alien, interdependent; high stone friction below, aerial traversal above.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
49. The Floating Peat Islands

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Scottish blanket bogs, Okavango wetlands, floating reed islands, and Baltic raised bogs.

Landscape: Mats of peat, moss, and root systems detach and migrate across a broad shallow basin. Old Nest foundations ride on some islands; others carry only rare flowers and companion life.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Wild World protects slow carbon and memory processes from constant extraction. Era One — Num markets prize unpredictable island movement and turn the bog into spectacle. Era Two — Market systems are removed; water level and core peat ecologies remain. Era Three — Settlements anchor islands seasonally, then release them to avoid exhausting one basin. During Hollow Seasons, several islands repeat an old commercial route despite local currents.

Present condition: Living, mobile, and vulnerable to drying.

Corruption: 3 in route behavior; 1 in ecology.

Aesthetic brief: Copper water, green-brown floating mats, mist, low flowers, stilt markers, and distant islands moving against the wind. Show motion through displaced wakes and taut anchor lines.

Background profile: Cool; Humid; bog/wetland; patient, mobile, melancholy; very low saturated-ground friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
50. The Patchwork Prairie of Broken Seasons

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: North American prairies, Eurasian steppe, Argentine pampas, and agricultural quilt landscapes.

Landscape: Adjacent fields occupy different seasonal states. One strip flowers in spring, one holds dry summer grass, one is under autumn storm, and one is winter-frozen. Boundaries follow old maintenance parcels rather than climate.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A broad ecology supports migration, fire, grazing, and long-distance weather. Era One — Seasonal management is divided into optimization zones. Era Two — Zones are folded together without fully reconciling their calendars. Era Three — Herds and communities learn routes that cross seasons in hours. Crops can be grown year-round, but diseases and parasites also move between cycles in unexpected ways.

Present condition: Productive and culturally diverse, with dangerous seasonal seams.

Corruption: 4.

Aesthetic brief: A wide readable horizon divided by irregular living boundaries rather than a simple grid. Flowers, gold grass, red storm light, and snow coexist. At a seam, rain may become falling leaves. Keep the foreground in one season per background variant for visual clarity.

Background profile: Variable temperature and humidity; prairie/farmland mosaic; abundant, restless, communal; medium grass or soil friction.

Why the broken seasons are surreal

The prairie replaces seasonal succession with physical adjacency. Spring flowers, dry summer grass, autumn storm light, and winter snow occupy neighboring maintenance parcels beneath one continuous horizon. A traveler can cross what should be months of change in a few hours because the old management zones were folded together without fully reconciling their calendars.

The boundaries are living ecological seams rather than a clean grid. Weather and matter can change meaning as they cross: rain may become falling leaves, crops can grow year-round, and diseases or parasites can move unexpectedly between cycles. The landscape remains productive and culturally diverse even while its calendar is physically broken.

Visual references — fullscreen 1920×1080

Asset folder: Patchwork Prairie of Broken Seasons

Each version includes a full background and six aligned parallax files: Sky, Far Background, Midground, Foreground B, Foreground A, and Walkable Floor.

Patchwork Prairie of Broken Seasons V1 — Spring foreground with summer, autumn, and winter parcels spreading across a broad shared horizon.

Patchwork Prairie of Broken Seasons V2 — Summer-gold foreground; rain changes into falling leaves where autumn and winter meet.

Patchwork Prairie of Broken Seasons V3 — Winter foreground opening through spring bloom toward summer grass and an autumn storm.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
51. The Sunken Terraces of Eris

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Southeast Asian rice terraces, Andean terraces, Pamukkale pools, and sunken gardens.

Landscape: Cultivation terraces descend into a huge circular basin. Lower rings are flooded and partly submerged; upper rings remain farms, orchards, and homes. Water carries fragments of old educational prompts that farmers treat as planting songs.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A House of Learning partners with an agricultural world so ecological education occurs through care work. Era One — Teaching prompts become standardized and detach from local practice. Era Two — The House is reduced into environmental affordances; terraces, water cycling, and several songs remain. Era Three — A structural collapse lowers the central rings. Communities adapt rather than abandon them, creating floating gardens and diving Paths.

Present condition: Productive, densely inhabited, and physically altered.

Corruption: 3.

Aesthetic brief: Green and gold terraces curving into turquoise flooded rings, white mineral edges, small bridges, orchard houses, and submerged classroom lights. The basin center should feel deep but calm, not like a catastrophe frozen in time.

Background profile: Warm; Moist-Humid; terrace farm/lake; industrious, harmonious, layered; high dry-path friction and low flooded-step friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
52. The Tundra Bloom Circuit

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Arctic tundra, Icelandic moss fields, Siberian permafrost polygons, and brief alpine wildflower blooms.

Landscape: A circular migratory route follows the rapid bloom of plants around a cold world. Ancient maintenance warmed small sections in sequence, creating a moving season rather than a fixed summer.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The circuit supports migratory companion life and communities that choose seasonal movement. Era One — Prediction makes the bloom perfectly punctual and reduces local adaptation. Era Two — Timing systems are simplified. Era Three — The bloom skips, doubles back, or pauses. Migrants interpret these changes through Path philosophy and must decide whether to follow tradition or current evidence.

Present condition: Mostly intact, increasingly irregular.

Corruption: 1–2.

Aesthetic brief: Low moss, polygon ground, snow patches, distant mountains, and intense small flowers forming a visible band across the landscape. One background variant can show dormant ground with the bloom approaching like color at the horizon.

Background profile: Freezing-Cold; Dry to Moist; tundra; fragile, hopeful, migratory; medium moss friction with low ice patches.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
53. The Volcanic Orchard Caldera

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Mediterranean terrace orchards, the Azores, Japanese volcanic farms, and Canary Island vineyards.

Landscape: Fruit-bearing organisms grow on black terraces inside an active caldera. Heat vents power healing baths and food processing, while old warning systems appear as colored blossoms.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Crafted/Wild community designs agriculture around volcanic succession instead of preventing every eruption. Era One — Medical correction and food optimization reduce crop variety. Era Two — Stewards preserve heat cycles, several heirloom fruits, and evacuation paths. Era Three — The warning grammar is partly lost. Communities know that silver flowers mean movement, but disagree whether red flowers predict ash, heat, or a maintenance reset.

Present condition: Fertile, inhabited, and periodically dangerous.

Corruption: 1–2.

Aesthetic brief: Black stone walls, vivid green terraces, white steam, bright fruit, a dark crater lake, and warning blossoms along paths. Corruption is expressed through mismatched bloom colors, not random lava glitches.

Background profile: Warm-Hot; Dry to Moist; volcanic orchard; cozy, productive, vigilant; high rough-stone friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
54. The Orchard of Borrowed Moons

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Terraced fruit orchards, East Asian moon-garden traditions, Mediterranean night agriculture, and observatory landscapes.

Landscape: Different orchard terraces operate under different preserved lunar cycles. Several moons can be visible at once, each governing flowering, pollination, or night behavior in its own zone.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Crafted World studies how shared agriculture changes when communities inhabit different time rhythms. Era One — The most productive moon cycles are copied across terraces, reducing diversity. Era Two — Incompatible cycles are folded together to preserve remaining pollinators. Era Three — Orchard keepers travel between moonlight zones and track identity by relationship rather than synchronized age. Some fruits ripen before their blossoms appear from the viewpoint of another terrace.

Present condition: Productive but temporally overlaid.

Corruption: 4.

Aesthetic brief: Dark terraced hills, silver leaves, blossoms in several colors, and multiple moons positioned over different horizon segments. Light boundaries should fall across paths like soft curtains. Avoid science-fiction machinery in the foreground; the time systems are embedded in sky and ecology.

Background profile: Cool-Neutral; Dry; nocturnal orchard; intimate, dreamlike, celebratory; medium soil friction.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
55. The Monsoon Stepwell City

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Indian stepwells, monsoon cities, cliff reservoirs, and terraced civic plazas.

Landscape: A city is built around enormous descending wells. In dry seasons they are markets and meeting spaces; in monsoon cycles they become vertical lakes connecting aquatic and land districts.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — An Open World city uses variable water level to ensure that civic space never belongs permanently to one body type. Era One — Optimization stabilizes water and privileges land districts. Era Two — Seasonal water variation is restored because it supports essential ecologies. Era Three — Several stepwells receive mismatched monsoon schedules from folded regions. Markets must move quickly, and submerged archives open only during high water.

Present condition: Crowded, adaptive, and partly overlaid.

Corruption: 4.

Aesthetic brief: Repeating geometric stairs, carved balconies, bright fabric canopies, deep green water, rain curtains, and boat bridges. A major-corruption well can be dry at the top while its lower reflection shows a flooded city from another season.

Background profile: Hot; Dry to Humid; civic reservoir; vibrant, cooperative, tense during transitions; high dry-stone friction and low wet-stair friction.

Why the seasons are surreal

The stepwell was built so that civic space would change ownership with the water level. Dry terraces, flooded routes, markets, archives, land districts, and aquatic districts were meant to exchange importance instead of allowing one body type to control the city permanently.

Era One stabilization weakened that design by privileging land districts. Era Two restored seasonal variation because the changing water supported essential ecologies, but folded regions now deliver mismatched monsoon schedules to different parts of the same city.

The result is not a simple weather anomaly. A dry stair may border a reflected flooded district, an archive may open only when another layer reaches high water, and markets must respond to several seasonal truths at once.

Visual references — fullscreen 1920×1080

Monsoon Stepwell City V1 — Monumental civic well, dry upper terrace, deep water districts, and seasonal reflection.

Monsoon Stepwell City V2 — Heavy rain, rising water, retreating markets, and temporary boat bridges.

Monsoon Stepwell City V3 — A split wet–dry transition with emerging archive doors and contradictory rainfall.

sources.label: Cyberpath Locations Atlas
sources.text:
56. The Urban Canyon Hive

Status: Proposed.

Real-world basis: Dense vertical cities, Mediterranean and Himalayan cliff settlements, canyon pueblos, elevated walkways, and layered transit hubs.

Landscape: Housing, workshops, Nests, and gardens occupy the walls of a former Era Zero transit canyon. Routes run horizontally, vertically, and across open space for many body forms.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Concordance junction is designed for continuous arrivals and body-specific navigation. Era One — Route standardization closes minor paths and concentrates status near major lines. Era Two — The junction loses long-distance travel but retains power, water, and shelter. Era Three — Migrants build outward from the infrastructure. When old routes briefly wake, entire walls become temporary streets and then close again.
